issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Stock class and specify a (static) stock attribute of type Stock, but the provided template implements the stock functionality in a class named Inventory (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Inventory.java) while Stock.java in the template is empty. The solution also uses Inventory as the stock type. This mismatch between the expected Stock type in the specification and the actual Inventory class in the template/solution will confuse students about which class/type to use and prevents following the specification literally.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the naming and types: either (A) update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock (so students use the provided Inventory class), or (B) provide a proper Stock implementation in the template (or rename Inventory to Stock) so the Stock type referenced in the specification actually exists. Ensure the static stock attribute type in the specification matches the concrete class in the template.

issues.description: The problem statement and class diagram refer to a Stock class (and a SealSaloon.stock attribute of type Stock), but the provided template and the solution use an Inventory class that implements the same API. This mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) names the same conceptual entity differently across artifacts and can confuse students about which class they should implement or modify.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the name across artifacts. Either (a) rename the Inventory class (and its file) to Stock in the template and solution and update all references (including SealSaloon.stock) to use Stock; or (b) update the problem statement and class diagram to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Ensure the file name and class name match (Stock.java/Stock or Inventory.java/Inventory) so students can clearly map requirements to the provided code.
